notes: Matched Nobel physics winners with named lunar craters, including Salam approved in 2024 and Skłodowska separately from Pierre Curie. This is a partial list: the complete gazetteer cross-check could not be performed, and November 2026 status has not been independently verified.

**Bragg** is an ancient [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is located on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"), just beyond the northwest limb. It dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-2) This formation has been heavily eroded and reshaped by subsequent impacts, leaving an irregular depression in the surface. The most intact portion of the rim is along the western face, while the northern and eastern rim has been nearly worn away and is overlaid by several smaller craters. The most notable of these is Bragg H, which lies across the east-southeastern rim.[[3]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-3): 36

This crater is located to the north-northwest of a [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Lorentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_(crater) "Lorentz (crater)"). Nearby craters of note include [Rynin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rynin_(crater) "Rynin (crater)") to the north, [Stefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_(crater) "Stefan (crater)") to the northwest, [Lacchini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacchini_(crater) "Lacchini (crater)") to the west, and [Avicenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna_(crater) "Avicenna (crater)") to the southeast.[[4]](#cite_note-LAC-36-4) The region about this crater is very rugged and marked by many smaller impacts.

This crater is named after English-Australian physicist [William H. Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Bragg "William Henry Bragg") (1862–1942),[[5]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-5) a 1915 [Nobel laureate in physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics "List of Nobel laureates in Physics") for his important work on [X-ray crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_crystallography "X-ray crystallography").[[6]](#cite_note-NobelBragg-6) Prior to its designation being formally adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970,[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1) Bragg was identified as *Crater 102*.[[7]](#cite_note-LFC-1A-7)

**Bragg** is an ancient [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is located on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"), just beyond the northwest limb. It dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-2) This formation has been heavily eroded and reshaped by subsequent impacts, leaving an irregular depression in the surface. The most intact portion of the rim is along the western face, while the northern and eastern rim has been nearly worn away and is overlaid by several smaller craters. The most notable of these is Bragg H, which lies across the east-southeastern rim.[[3]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-3): 36

This crater is located to the north-northwest of a [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Lorentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_(crater) "Lorentz (crater)"). Nearby craters of note include [Rynin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rynin_(crater) "Rynin (crater)") to the north, [Stefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_(crater) "Stefan (crater)") to the northwest, [Lacchini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacchini_(crater) "Lacchini (crater)") to the west, and [Avicenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna_(crater) "Avicenna (crater)") to the southeast.[[4]](#cite_note-LAC-36-4) The region about this crater is very rugged and marked by many smaller impacts.

This crater is named after English-Australian physicist [William H. Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Bragg "William Henry Bragg") (1862–1942),[[5]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-5) a 1915 [Nobel laureate in physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics "List of Nobel laureates in Physics") for his important work on [X-ray crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_crystallography "X-ray crystallography").[[6]](#cite_note-NobelBragg-6) Prior to its designation being formally adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970,[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1) Bragg was identified as *Crater 102*.[[7]](#cite_note-LFC-1A-7)

**Bragg** is an ancient [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is located on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon"), just beyond the northwest limb. It dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-2) This formation has been heavily eroded and reshaped by subsequent impacts, leaving an irregular depression in the surface. The most intact portion of the rim is along the western face, while the northern and eastern rim has been nearly worn away and is overlaid by several smaller craters. The most notable of these is Bragg H, which lies across the east-southeastern rim.[[3]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-3): 36

This crater is located to the north-northwest of a [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Lorentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_(crater) "Lorentz (crater)"). Nearby craters of note include [Rynin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rynin_(crater) "Rynin (crater)") to the north, [Stefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_(crater) "Stefan (crater)") to the northwest, [Lacchini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacchini_(crater) "Lacchini (crater)") to the west, and [Avicenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna_(crater) "Avicenna (crater)") to the southeast.[[4]](#cite_note-LAC-36-4) The region about this crater is very rugged and marked by many smaller impacts.

This crater is named after English-Australian physicist [William H. Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Bragg "William Henry Bragg") (1862–1942),[[5]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-5) a 1915 [Nobel laureate in physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics "List of Nobel laureates in Physics") for his important work on [X-ray crystallography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray_crystallography "X-ray crystallography").[[6]](#cite_note-NobelBragg-6) Prior to its designation being formally adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970,[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1) Bragg was identified as *Crater 102*.[[7]](#cite_note-LFC-1A-7)

## More in Space & Astronomy

### Every orbital and deep-space launch since Sputnik

Every launch attempt that aimed to reach Earth orbit or beyond, from Sputnik 1 in 1957 to the present, with date, rocket, launch site, launch provider, country and outcome. One row per launch attempt.

### Confirmed exoplanets

Every confirmed planet outside the Solar System in the NASA Exoplanet Archive, with its host star, discovery details, orbit, size, mass and temperature. One row per planet.

### Orbital launches by country and year

Number of orbital and deep-space launch attempts per country per year since 1957, split into successes and failures, with the payload mass delivered to orbit. One row per country per year.

### Gravitational-wave detections (LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA)

Every confident gravitational-wave signal from merging black holes and neutron stars in the cumulative LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA catalog (GWTC), from GW150914 in 2015 onward, with the masses of the two objects, the remnant mass, distance, redshift and signal strength. One row per merger event.

### Asteroids with known rotation periods

Every asteroid in NASA JPL's Small-Body Database with a listed rotation period (how long it takes to spin once), with orbit class, size, brightness and distance from the Sun. One row per asteroid.

### Near-Earth asteroids first observed in 2021 or later

Every known near-Earth asteroid whose earliest recorded observation falls in 2021 or later, with orbit class, size, Earth MOID and orbital elements. One row per asteroid.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Main article: [List of craters on the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon")

The list of approved names in the *[Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature")* maintained by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") includes the diameter of the crater and the person the crater is named for.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Where a crater formation has associated [satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite") craters, these are detailed on the main crater description pages.

The list of approved names in the *[Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature")* maintained by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") includes the diameter of the crater and the person the crater is named for.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Where a crater formation has associated [satellite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite "Satellite") craters, these are detailed on the main crater description pages.

**Hess** is a degraded [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies in the southern hemisphere on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon").[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-1) On the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale"), Hess dates from the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period.[[2]](#cite_note-Purohit_et_al_2018-2) The crater rim has been worn by subsequent impacts, leaving a low, eroded outer wall. The flat interior has been resurfaced by [lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava "Lava") flows and is free of significant impacts. This floor has a slightly darker [albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") than the surrounding terrain.

The crater [Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle_(crater) "Boyle (crater)") is nearly attached to the northeastern rim of Hess, and [Abbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbe_(crater) "Abbe (crater)") lies to the south. To the west is a large [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") named [Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_(crater) "Poincaré (crater)"), and Hess is located at the eastern edge of the crater's deeply eroded outer rim. The satellite crater Hess Z is partly overlaid by the northern rim of Hess. The small crater Hess M joins the south-southwest rim of Hess to the northwest rim of Abbe.

By convention these features are identified on lunar maps by placing the letter on the side of the crater midpoint that is closest to Hess.

![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/Raman_crater_4157_h3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)

**Raman** is a small [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies on the western edge of a plateau feature in the expansive [lunar mare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_mare "Lunar mare") named [Oceanus Procellarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanus_Procellarum "Oceanus Procellarum"). It shares this plateau with the [lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava "Lava")-flooded [Herodotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus_(crater) "Herodotus (crater)") and [Aristarchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristarchus_(crater) "Aristarchus (crater)") to the southeastern. To the northeast of Raman is the small peak named [Mons Herodotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mons_Herodotus "Mons Herodotus"). To the northwest on the mare is the long, narrow range named the [Montes Agricola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montes_Agricola "Montes Agricola").

This is an elongated crater formation, with a secondary feature bulging out along the southeast rim. The inner walls of this crater have a higher [albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") than the surrounding [terrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrain "Terrain"), which is indicative of a relatively youthful formation. This crater was previously designated Herodotus D,[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_Rees_2014-1) a satellite crater of Herodotus, before being named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union").

**Chadwick** is a [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon")'s surface, just beyond the southwestern limb. It lies to the northwest of the crater [De Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Roy_(crater) "De Roy (crater)"), within the [Mendel-Rydberg Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendel-Rydberg_Basin "Mendel-Rydberg Basin"), a 630 km wide impact basin of [Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nectarian "Nectarian") age.[[2]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-2) Further to the northwest of Chadwick is the larger crater [Mendel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendel_(lunar_crater) "Mendel (lunar crater)").[[3]](#cite_note-LAC-135-3) This region of the lunar surface lies at the southern end of the ejecta blanket that surrounds the [Mare Orientale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") impact basin.

Chadwick is roughly circular with a sharp-edged rim. The inner wall is somewhat wider to the south-southeast, giving the crater a slight outward bulge toward De Roy. The rim has not been significantly worn, and is not marked by any impacts of note. The interior surface has a somewhat uneven appearance.[[4]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-4) The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase "Plagioclase") has been identified on the northeast, southeast, and south walls, as well as an unnamed crater to the southwest.[[5]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-5)

Previously designated De Roy X,[[4]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-4) this crater is named after British physicist [James Chadwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Chadwick "James Chadwick") (1891-1974), the 1935 [Nobel laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") for his [discovery of the neutron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_the_neutron "Discovery of the neutron"). Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1985.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Michelson_crater_5024_h1.jpg/250px-Michelson_crater_5024_h1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michelson_crater_5024_h1.jpg)

A view of Michelson from [Lunar Orbiter 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Orbiter_5 "Lunar Orbiter 5"), facing west

**Michelson** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-1) It lies along the northeastern outer rim of a huge [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Hertzsprung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertzsprung_(crater) "Hertzsprung (crater)"), and to the southwest of the crater [Kolhörster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolhörster_(crater) "Kolhörster (crater)").

This is a heavily eroded crater formation with multiple impacts along the rim edge and within the interior. The rim is roughly circular, but has been rendered relatively uneven due to these smaller craters. There are small craters across the interior floor, including impacts along the northern, western and southeastern edges. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase "Plagioclase") has been identified on the southwest floor.[[2]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-2)

To the southeast of the outer rim is a crater chain that has been designated Catena Michelson. This feature is radial to the [Mare Orientale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") impact basin, and passes near the outer rim of the crater [Grachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grachev_(crater) "Grachev (crater)").
